content_html:
Mealybugs appear as small insects or white waxy masses around nodes, leaf axils, and undersides, and they may leave sticky honeydew. To recover a plant, isolate it, confirm where the pests are concentrated, and combine physical removal with a compatible treatment if needed. Reinspection matters because hidden colonies return if only the visible insects are cleaned once.

Isolate and inspect nodes, leaf axils, and hidden areas

Check leaf joints, petiole bases, stems, and, for some species, accessible roots. Ants around the plant may be attracted to honeydew. Inspect plants that were touching it before grouping them together again.

Remove visible clusters without damaging tissue

For a small infestation, a swab or damp cloth can remove visible clusters; prune heavily colonized parts only if the plant can tolerate it. Do not scrape tender stems or soak potting mix with products not intended for that use.

Use labeled products and test compatibility

Insecticidal soaps or horticultural oils can be contact options for certain plants. Follow the label, reach hiding places, and test an inconspicuous area because some foliage is sensitive. Do not mix household treatments or increase concentration to speed results.

Inspect for weeks and manage honeydew

Clean sticky surfaces and look for new white masses every few days. Healthy new growth and no new colonies indicate recovery. An infestation spread across many plants or into roots may justify nursery or professional advice for valuable collections.
